analysis.one_liner: Shields respirator makers and sellers from defective-design and warning lawsuits over federally approved devices.
analysis.headline: The bill died in House committees without ever receiving a vote, despite 27 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have barred any lawsuit claiming a respirator's design or warning labels were defective, as long as the device carried a federal NIOSH safety approval. It would have overridden all state and local laws on those claims and applied retroactively to any case that had not yet reached trial. Its stated purpose was to keep litigation costs from driving respirator makers out of business.
analysis.who_benefits: Respirator manufacturers and the retailers, distributors, and wholesalers who sell their products gain near-total immunity from design and warning-defect lawsuits, including for cases already filed in court. They would remain liable only if a device failed to comply with its approved design.

how_it_helps.text: A manufacturer or seller could not be sued for defective design or warning if the respirator had NIOSH approval and was built to the approved design and labeling; the shield would apply even to lawsuits already in court that had not yet reached trial.

The bill's findings argue that litigation costs could push manufacturers to stop making respirators, and that continued US respirator production is needed to protect workers and emergency responders in disasters and epidemics.
The bill would supersede any state or local law on such claims, giving manufacturers a single federal standard instead of state court liability rules.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and responders injured by a respirator whose federally approved design or warnings proved inadequate would lose their day in court, including people whose lawsuits were already underway when the bill took effect. State courts and state product-liability laws would also lose authority over these claims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Injured workers suing over approved respirators

drawbacks.text: The bill would have wiped out pending lawsuits that had not reached trial, closing the courthouse door on workers already injured by respirators they trusted.

A NIOSH approval certifies that a design met minimum federal standards at the time of testing; the bill would have barred juries from finding that a minimally compliant design or warning was nonetheless unreasonably dangerous for real-world use, eliminating a check that operates beyond what regulators require.

Manufacturers who cannot control how their products are used would keep immunity even where a user's harm stemmed from warnings the manufacturer itself wrote, since the shield covers defective-warning claims for NIOSH-approved labeling.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's premise—litigation costs could shrink the supply of protective respirators—has some force, and it would not have immunized devices that violated their approved design. But the trade it offered was one-sided: manufacturers and sellers got a nearly complete liability shield, while injured workers, including those with cases already in court, got nothing in return and lost their ability to hold anyone accountable for an approved-but-flawed design or warning.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees, sent to the Energy and Commerce Health Subcommittee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Shuster introduced the bill on May 12, 2005, joined by Reps. Holden, Hart, and Smith of Texas.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and to Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced; on May 23, 2005, it went to Energy and Commerce's Subcommittee on Health, where it stayed.
The bill accumulated 27 cosponsors, 19 Republicans and 8 Democrats, but no committee action followed and it died when the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured workers and their families came out ahead: the bill never became law, so state courts kept jurisdiction and workers retained the right to sue over defective respirator designs and warnings. Respirator makers failed to get the liability shield they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured workers who kept their right to sue

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship skewed Republican—19 of 27 cosponsors were Republicans—but the bill's original cosponsors included a Democrat, and no roll-call votes ever occurred.

industries.note: The bill would have given makers of NIOSH-approved respirators immunity from defective-design and defective-warning lawsuits, including suits already in court. Their gain would have come directly at the expense of workers injured by approved devices.
Sellers of all kinds—retailers, distributors, wholesalers—were covered by the same immunity, ending their exposure to liability for respirators they merely sold.
The bill would have eliminated an entire category of product-liability claims, closing off the legal remedy workers use when safety equipment fails them.
